questions.question: Nadia does 40 trials. In each trial she flips a coin (heads or tails) and spins a spinner that lands on green or yellow. She records the results in a table with four rows: heads and green happened 11 times, heads and yellow happened 9 times, tails and green happened 12 times, tails and yellow happened 8 times. That is 40 trials in all. What is the experimental probability of getting tails and yellow?
questions.explain: Experimental probability = how many times that pair happened divided by the total number of trials, so it is 8/40 (which is 1/5). The common trap is using 8/20 by dividing by only the 20 tails trials — the whole is always every trial you ran.

questions.question: In each trial, Owen spins a spinner that lands on red or blue and then flips a coin. After 60 trials his table shows: red and heads 18 times, red and tails 14 times, blue and heads 13 times, blue and tails 15 times. What is the experimental probability of red and heads?
questions.explain: Take the count for the red-and-heads pair, 18, and divide by all 60 trials: 18/60 = 3/10. Two traps to avoid are dividing by the 32 red trials instead of 60, and answering 1/4 from what you expect instead of from the data you actually collected.

questions.question: Kai runs 25 trials. Each trial is spinning a spinner that lands on Bus or Bike and flipping a coin. His table shows: Bus and heads 6 times, Bus and tails 7 times, Bike and heads 5 times, Bike and tails 7 times, for 25 trials in all. What is the experimental probability of Bike and heads, written as a percent?
questions.explain: Bike and heads happened 5 times out of 25 trials, and 5/25 = 0.2 = 20%. The usual trap is dividing by the 12 Bike trials or the 11 heads trials — the denominator of an experimental probability is the total number of trials.

questions.question: Priya flips a penny and a dime together. One trial is flipping both coins once, and she does 80 trials. Her table shows: two heads 22 times, heads then tails 18 times, tails then heads 21 times, two tails 19 times. What is the experimental probability of getting two heads?
questions.explain: Two heads came up 22 times out of 80 trials, so the experimental probability is 22/80 = 11/40. A frequent trap is writing 22/58 by comparing the 22 successes with the 58 other trials instead of with all 80.

questions.question: In a board game, you move forward if a trial gives green and heads, or if it gives purple and tails. A trial is spinning a green/purple spinner and flipping a coin. After 50 trials the table shows: green and heads 12 times, green and tails 14 times, purple and heads 11 times, purple and tails 13 times. What is the experimental probability of moving forward?
questions.explain: Add the counts of both winning pairs first, 12 + 13 = 25, then divide by the 50 trials: 25/50 = 1/2. The classic trap is writing 12/50 + 13/50 and adding the denominators too, which gives 25/100 — denominators stay the same when the whole is the same 50 trials.

questions.question: Two groups spin the same blue/orange spinner and flip the same coin. Group A ran 20 trials and got blue and heads 9 times, so they report 0.45. Group B ran 200 trials and got blue and heads 46 times, so they report 0.23. Which estimate of the probability of blue and heads should the class trust more, and why?
options: Group A's 0.45, because 9 out of 20 already shows blue and heads happens a lot.
Group B's 0.23, because an experimental probability found from 200 trials is more reliable than one from 20 trials.
Group A's 0.45, because a small number of trials is easier to record without making mistakes.
Neither — you must average the two results and report 0.34.
questions.explain: The more trials you run, the closer the experimental probability usually settles to the true probability, so the 200-trial result is the better estimate. The trap is trusting a small batch like 20 trials just because the fraction looks convincing.

questions.question: A trial is spinning a spinner labelled Apple or Berry and flipping a coin. In 100 trials, the table shows Apple and heads 27 times, Apple and tails 24 times, and Berry and heads 23 times. The Berry and tails row got smudged. What is the experimental probability of Berry and tails, as a percent?
questions.explain: First find the missing count: 100 - (27 + 24 + 23) = 26, then divide by the total, 26/100 = 26%. Answering 25% means using what you expect from four equally likely pairs instead of the counts you actually recorded.

questions.question: Ravi and Sofia test the same two events: drawing a marble from a bag and putting it back, then flipping a coin. Ravi ran 40 trials and got red and heads 9 times. Sofia ran 60 trials and got red and heads 15 times. Using all of their trials together, what is the experimental probability of red and heads?
questions.explain: Pool the results: 9 + 15 = 24 successes out of 40 + 60 = 100 trials, so 24/100 = 6/25. The trap is mixing one person's count with the other person's number of trials — the top and the bottom of the fraction must come from the same set of trials.

questions.question: Ella flips a coin and spins a red/blue spinner. In 8 trials she gets heads and red 4 times, so she calculates 4/8 = 1/2. She says the spinner and coin must be rigged toward heads and red. What is the best thing for her to do next?
options: Run many more trials, because with only 8 trials the experimental probability can land far from the true probability.
Agree with her: 1/2 is the true probability of heads and red, because that is what her trials show.
Stop and report 1/2, because 8 trials is already enough to be sure about heads and red.
Throw out the 4 heads-and-red trials so the results look fair.
questions.explain: Experimental probability from a handful of trials bounces around a lot, so the fix is more trials, not a conclusion — after 100 or 200 trials the fraction usually settles down. The trap is treating a lucky streak in 8 trials as proof that something is rigged.

questions.question: Maya flips a coin and spins a red/blue spinner 30 times. To save time she writes down only the 16 trials that came up heads: heads and red 9 times, heads and blue 7 times. She reports the experimental probability of heads and red as 9/16. What is the correct experimental probability, and why?
options: 9/16, because those are the only trials where heads and red could have happened.
3/10, because all 30 trials she ran belong in the total.
1/4, because heads and red is one of the four possible pairs.
16/30, because that is how often heads came up in her trials.
questions.explain: Every trial counts in the denominator, so it is 9 successes out of 30 trials = 3/10. Filtering the table down to just the heads trials shrinks the whole and makes the probability look bigger than it really is.

questions.question: Five students in a Grade 7 class each run 24 trials of the same experiment: spin a blue/yellow spinner, then flip a coin. Across the whole class, blue and tails came up 36 times. What is the experimental probability of blue and tails, as a percent?
questions.explain: Find the total trials first, 5 x 24 = 120, then divide: 36/120 = 0.3 = 30%. Two traps are reading the count 36 as if it were already a percent, and doubling the total to 240 because each trial involves two events — one trial is one spin plus one flip.

questions.question: Jade runs 200 trials. In each trial she flips a coin and spins a spinner that lands on star or moon. Her table shows heads and star 38 times out of the 200 trials. Which statement is best supported by her data?
options: In her first 6 trials heads and star never appeared, so its experimental probability is 0.
Her friend did 5 extra flips and spins and got heads and star 3 times, so the probability is really 60%.
Because 38 is far from 50, the coin result must be changing what the spinner lands on.
The experimental probability of heads and star is 19%, and running even more trials would probably change it only a little.
questions.explain: Use all the trials: 38/200 = 0.19 = 19%, and a result built from 200 trials is fairly stable. The trap is letting 5 or 6 trials overrule 200 — tiny samples swing wildly and cannot replace a large set of trials.
